newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Midwest power continues retreat on weather.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Midwest power continues retreat on weather.

text.p: Wholesale U.S. Midwest spot electricity prices were lower again Monday after retreating by about $20 Friday, ladened by warmer-than-expected temperatures moving into most of the region and softer natural gas prices.

Despite expectations for more bitterly cold weather this week in the Midwest, forecasters are now calling for slightly milder temperatures through the early part of next week, with only patches of cold in the northern plains.

In the Mid-Continent Area Power Pool (MAPP), where temperatures remain below-normal, peak non-firm power prices were still in the $17.00-18.00 per megawatt hour (MWh) range for Tuesday delivery but down around $15.00 for Wednesday.
Off-peak non-firm MAPP power deals were still assessed at $12.50-14.00.
In the Mid-American Interpool Network (MAIN), peak, non-firm power prices for Tuesday delivery were in the $15.00-16.00 range, down from the $23.25-24.25 range seen on Friday.
MAIN off peak power was notionally assessed in the $10.50-11.50 range, down about $1.50 from Friday.
Peak, non-firm electricity prices in the East Central Area Reliability Coordination Agreement (ECAR) for Tuesday were in the $10.00-12.00 range, as compared with Friday's $17.25-18.25 trading range.
January/February ECAR prices were mostly steady in the $25.00-26.00 range as most traders were leaving forward business on the backburner.
Off-peak, non-firm next-day ECAR power was notionally talked flat in the $12.00-14.00 range, as some buyers were short supply, sources said.

In the Southwest Power Pool (SPP), where temperatures are expected to climb to about eight to 15 degrees above-normal by Friday, peak non-firm power for Tuesday delivery continued to falter, dipping into the $14.00-15.00 range, down from the $18.00-19.00 area on Friday.
January/February peak prices in SPP were about 50 cents lower in the $25.00-26.00 area.
Off-peak prices throughout SPP were notionally around $11.75.

Contributing to the weaker electricity prices were the significantly lower natural gas prices. In the Midcontinent, gas for Tuesday delivery traded mostly in the low-$3.90s, down about 40 cents from Friday.

Separately, Commonwealth Edison's 794 megawatt (MW) Dresden 2 nuclear unit was reduced to about 40 percent power early Monday morning. The company said the unit would run at reduced power, no higher than 70 percent, until repairs were complete on a turbine control valve.
ComEd's other unit (Dresden 3), with an identical generating capacity, is expected to return to service later this week.
